opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot. The short answer is that each new city gets meaningfully easier, but not because we just copy and paste what we did before.

When we started in Phoenix, and then expanded to San Francisco and Los Angeles, a lot of the work was building the foundation: the core perception, prediction, and planning stack, and learning how to handle the long tail of situations you only see once you've driven many miles. Every city teaches you something. San Francisco has dense urban driving, lots of pedestrians and cyclists, hills, fog, and double-parked delivery trucks. Phoenix has wide roads, higher speeds, and different weather. Los Angeles has its own freeway culture and traffic patterns. All of that experience goes back into one shared driver. We don't build a separate system per city; we build one system that generalizes better and better.

So when we go somewhere new, most of what the car needs to know already transfers. A pedestrian is a pedestrian, a cyclist behaves roughly like a cyclist, and the fundamentals of driving carry over. What remains is the delta: local road geometry, unusual signage or lane markings, local driving norms like how assertive people are at merges or unprotected turns, specific weather conditions, and the occasional truly novel situation. Much of our work is identifying that delta quickly and efficiently.

That's where our tooling matters. We have strong simulation, evaluation frameworks, and data mining pipelines, so we can drive in a new city, find where the system's behavior differs from what we want, and focus on those cases instead of re-validating everything from scratch. Increasingly, larger and more capable models, including ones that benefit from broad pretraining and world knowledge, help here too. They generalize better to things the system hasn't seen many times before.

There's also a lot of non-technical learning that transfers: how we work with cities, first responders, and regulators, how we roll out to riders, how we operate depots and fleets. That playbook has matured a lot.

So I'd say the effort to launch a new city has dropped substantially, and the timeline from first driving to serving riders keeps shrinking. But we still hold a very high safety bar, so we do the local validation carefully. The goal is for the generalization to keep improving so that each new place is mostly about confirming what we expect, plus targeted work on whatever is genuinely new.

r001.rationale: The response describes varied conditions learned across Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles, then says that experience improves one shared driver’s ability to generalize so most of its capabilities transfer to new cities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that it changes almost everything about how we approach it. When we launched in Phoenix, and then San Francisco, each of those felt like a research project in a sense. We were learning what the long tail of driving actually looks like in a dense urban environment, what kinds of behaviors from pedestrians and cyclists and other drivers we hadn't anticipated, how weather and road geometry and local driving culture interact with the system.

What's happened over the last couple of years is that the Waymo Driver has become much more general. A big part of that is the shift toward large, end-to-end-ish learned models that absorb a lot of driving experience across all the places we operate. So when we go to a new city, we're not starting from scratch. The model already has a very strong prior on how to drive. Most of the behaviors transfer. Los Angeles and Austin and Atlanta, for example, came up dramatically faster than San Francisco did, and that's not because those cities are easy. It's because the system had already seen most of what it needed to see.

So the work in a new city shifts from "teach the car to drive here" to "validate that it drives here safely." We still do mapping, we still collect data, we still have a period where we drive with autonomous specialists in the vehicle. But the emphasis is on evaluation. We're looking for the deltas: what's different about this city? Maybe it's a particular kind of intersection geometry, maybe it's how people use turn lanes, maybe it's a lot more freeway driving, or in a place like Tokyo, driving on the other side of the road with a very different signage and pedestrian culture. We want to find those differences early, measure how the driver handles them, and close any gaps, often through simulation rather than having to go out and drive millions of real-world miles.

The other thing experience gives you is a much better evaluation methodology. We've built up a very rich understanding of what matters for safety, what the rare but important scenarios are, and how to construct simulated tests that stress the system in those ways. That infrastructure is reusable. So I'd say the research has gotten more exciting, actually, because the questions are now about generalization and about scaling the evaluation, rather than about getting the basics right in each individual place.

r001.rationale: The response says the Driver has absorbed experience across operating locations, has a stronger prior, and transfers most behaviors to new cities because it has already encountered much of what it needs to handle.

astra-6.text:
I think the experience carries over quite a bit. You’re not starting from scratch with every new city. A lot of the driving capabilities—understanding other road users, navigating intersections, handling complex traffic—are shared across cities. And as you encounter more variation, you build a system that can handle a broader range of situations.

But that doesn’t mean a new city is just a switch you flip. You still need to understand what’s different: the road layouts, local driving behavior, weather, and the kinds of unusual situations you might encounter. Then you need to test and validate that the system handles those differences well.

So the work increasingly becomes identifying and addressing those differences, rather than rebuilding the driving capability. And experience helps with the launch process itself, too—you get better at knowing what to look for and how to evaluate readiness.

r001.rationale: The response says that experience across more variation builds a system that handles a broader range of situations, and that shared capabilities carry over to new cities, making deployment easier than starting from scratch.

sol-6.1.text:
The experience carries over quite a bit. We’re not building a new driver from scratch for each city. As we encounter different road layouts, traffic patterns, and behaviors, we improve the system, and those improvements can help us in the next city as well.

But there’s still work to understand what’s different locally. Are there unusual intersections, different driving conventions, or conditions that we haven’t seen enough of? We need to test those and validate that the system handles them safely. So the goal is for each launch to build on the previous ones, with more of the capability transferring and the remaining work focused on those local differences.

r001.rationale: The response says that experience with different road layouts, traffic patterns, and behaviors improves the system and helps it work in the next city, communicating that broader prior exposure supports transfer to new cities.
